desc:
A connected, weighted, undirected graph has n nodes numbered 0 to n - 1; edges[i] = [a, b, w] is an edge between a and b of weight w. A spanning tree is a set of n - 1 edges (identified by their positions in the list) that connects all nodes.

List the total weights of all spanning trees in non-decreasing order, one entry per tree, so equal weights may appear several times. Return the second entry of this list. If the graph has only one spanning tree, return -1.

n = 4, edges = [[0,1,1],[1,2,2],[2,3,3],[0,3,4]]   -> 7
(trees: 6 [edges 0,1,2], 7 [0,1,3], 8 [0,2,3], 9 [1,2,3])

If two different trees both have the minimum weight, the answer equals the minimum weight.
constraints: edges[i] = [a, b, w] with 0 ≤ a, b < n and a ≠ b
The graph is connected; parallel edges are allowed
hints: Start with a minimum spanning tree T of weight W. How could a different spanning tree look if it is as close to T as possible?
A second-best tree can always be obtained from T by a single swap: add one non-tree edge e = (a, b) and remove the heaviest tree edge on the path from a to b.

So the answer is the minimum of W + w(e) - maxOnPath(a, b) over all non-tree edges e. To get maxOnPath for all pairs quickly, record the weight whenever Kruskal merges two components: every pair (x in A, y in B) gets that weight as its maximum on the tree path.
editorial: Build an MST T with Kruskal's algorithm and let W be its weight. Every other spanning tree differs from T, and a classical exchange argument shows that the cheapest tree different from T can be reached by a single swap: insert a non-tree edge e = (a, b), which closes a cycle through the tree path from a to b, and delete the heaviest edge on that path. The resulting weight is W + w(e) - maxOnPath(a, b).

If several MSTs exist, some swap has difference 0 and the formula returns W, matching the definition. If there are no non-tree edges, T is the only spanning tree and the answer is -1. To get maxOnPath(a, b), note that when Kruskal merges components A and B with an edge of weight c, the tree path between any x in A and y in B has the merge edge as its heaviest one (all other edges were added earlier and are not heavier). Filling a matrix this way costs O(n²) in total, since every pair is assigned exactly once. Overall: O(m log m + n²).
